newsitem.title: USA: "Megan's Law" killer faces trial for his life.
newsitem.headline: "Megan's Law" killer faces trial for his life.

text.p: The jury that convicted Jesse Timmendequas last month for the rape and murder of 7-year-old Megan Kanka in July 1994 returns Monday to hear testimony on whether he should be executed or live out his life behind bars.

In the case that led "Megan's Law", the statute aimed at informing the public about convicted sex offenders in their midst, the jury will be asked to decide whether Timmendequas should become the 14th inmate on New Jersey's Death Row.

Public Defender Barbara Lependorf has argued that Timmendequas was easily influenced, that his two housemates' movements during the critical minutes were not accounted for and that his incriminating statements may have led to his taking the blame for actions that were not his.
After the jury's verdict she pointed out Timmendequas would not pose a threat since he will remain behind bars without parole under new state law.

First Assistant Prosecutor Kathryn Flicker was expected to stress that the 36-year-old defendant confessed to luring the girl to the Hamilton Township house where he was living to see a puppy. Once inside he raped her, strangled her and put her head in plastic bags.
She said the murder was meant to cover up the rape.
The prosecutor laid the ground for the death penalty. "He meant to kill. He chose to kill," she told the jury.

The crime touched off a public outcry, led by parents Maureen and Richard Kanka who said they hadn't known their neighbour was a twice-convicted sex offender. Now "Megan's Law" requires offenders to register and empowers the authorities to notify the public about those they conclude pose a high risk.
The crime not only attracted national media attention but made Megan's Law a nationwide model for sex offenders policy.
